newsitem.title: USA: Zitel sees payoff from "year 2000" unit.
newsitem.headline: Zitel sees payoff from "year 2000" unit.

text.p: Zitel Corp president Jack King said the firm expected do well from its relationship with MatriDigm Corp, a firm that Zitel helped found which will soon begin marketing a proprietary system to fix the "year 2000 problem" in computers.

"If in fact they'll deliver what they purport to deliver, and stay within their business model...they'll do right well (and) I expect we'll do well as well," King told an Emerald Asset Management investment seminar.
Zitel helped found MatriDigm in 1995, and owns a 33 percent equity stake. It also is a licensed reseller of MatriDigm services.
MatriDigm has developed an automated technique for finding and correcting in IBM mainframe software language program code that fails to correctly recognize the year 2000.

The widespread presence of such code, in which years are expressed in two digits rather than four and thus make computers incorrectly interpret 2000, is expected to cost $250 billion to $400 billion to correct, King said.

King said the MatriDigm "code conversion factory," which is based on previously developed technology for "maintaining" computer code, will be available to customers beginning next week and has performed well in tests.
For example, he said, the system was able to correctly identify as months of the year data fields the original programmer had named after his previous girlfriends rather than the actual month names.
The system is able to convert one million lines of code per hour, King said.
In addition, MatriDigm will continue to have strong prospects after the year 2000 in maintaining the billions of lines of computer code written for IBM mainframe computers, King said.
"Their business will be a growing business," he said.
